title: Where to Find a Spouse: Marriage Map Pinpoints the Best Areas
gist: New IFS 'Where to find your spouse' maps show that neighborhoods with the most singles (eastern Cleveland, Detroit, Philadelphia, Chicago) are not where marriages actually happen; instead, marriage formation clusters in middle-America metros like Provo, UT and Fort Wayne, IN, and is best predicted by the local ratio of employed single men to single women rather than the sheer number of singles.

themes.theme: Singles density vs. actual marriage formation

insights.claim: The neighborhoods with the highest share of unmarried adults ages 22-39 are concentrated in urban areas — eastern Cleveland and part of Detroit top the list at 87% unmarried — with the rest of the top 10 in Detroit, Philadelphia, Chicago, Louisville, Milwaukee, and Washington, D.C., all above 80% unmarried.
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: High single-population density in a city is not evidence of a strong marriage market — the opposite pattern holds, which matters for anyone using 'most singles' as a proxy for dating/marriage opportunity.
insights.quote: In eastern Cleveland and part of Detroit, 87% of young adults ages 22 to 39 are not married, the highest in the country.
insights.locator: finding 1, 'places with the most single adults'

insights.claim: The areas with the most new marriages are concentrated in middle America — near Provo, UT; Fort Wayne and Evansville, IN; and Colorado Springs, CO — plus West/Central Tennessee, Northwest Georgia, North Carolina's Greenville/Jacksonville corridor, and parts of Texas and Florida.
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Contradicts the assumption that big coastal/urban singles scenes are the best marriage markets — investors/operators in dating or relocation-adjacent services should weight middle-America metros more heavily.
insights.quote: The areas with the most new marriages are almost entirely in middle America

insights.claim: Provo, Utah has the nation's highest marriage rate: an average of 132 first-time marriages per year for every 1,000 never-married adults ages 22-39 from 2020-2024, followed by Fort Wayne, IN (106) and Evansville, IN (94) per 1,000.
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Quantifies just how large the marriage-rate gap is across US metros (Provo's rate is roughly 40% higher than the next-closest area), useful as a benchmark for regional family-formation forecasting.
insights.quote: Provo has the highest marriage rate in the country. From 2020 to 2024, an average of 132 first-time marriages were formed each year for every 1,000 never-married adults ages 22-39.

insights.claim: Lakewood Township, Ocean County, NJ — an area with a large Orthodox Jewish population — has the highest share of currently-married young adults (over 73% of those ages 22-39), followed closely by parts of Utah such as west Utah county (72%).
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Religious/cultural community density (Orthodox Jewish, Mormon) is a stronger correlate of being married than urban density or income alone — a durable, non-economic driver of family formation.
insights.quote: the Lakewood Township area of Ocean County, New Jersey, with a large Orthodox Jewish population, stands out as the top area. More than 73% of adults in their twenties and thirties in this area are married.

themes.theme: The employed-single-men ratio as the real marriage-market driver

insights.claim: There is a strong link between new marriages in an area and the ratio of full-time employed single men to single women (ages 22-39), using grouped Public Use Microdata Areas (PUMAs) of at least 500,000 people.
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, replicable metric — employed single men per 100 single women — that outperforms raw population or urbanicity for predicting where marriages will actually form; usable as a screening variable for relocation, real estate, or dating-product targeting.
insights.quote: we find a strong link between the new marriages in an area and the ratio of full-time employed single men to single women

insights.claim: The two areas with the highest ratios of employed single men to single women (North Dakota and the area around San Jose, CA) both have marriage rates in the upper 20% range, while the two lowest-ratio areas (middle Manhattan and south of Chicago) both have marriage rates in the lower 20% range.
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Illustrates the practical spread implied by the employed-men ratio: it separates high- and low-marriage-rate areas by roughly a 20-point range at the extremes.

insights.claim: For unmarried adults in their 20s, the highest employed-single-men-to-women ratios are found near major military bases — Jacksonville City (NC), East Cumberland County (NC), and El Paso Teller (CO) — because bases create large populations of young, employed men relative to single women.
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Military-base-adjacent communities are structurally favorable marriage markets for women in their 20s due to labor-force gender composition, not affordability or culture per se.
insights.quote: nearly every top area is anchored by a major military installation, which creates unusually large populations of young, full-time-employed men and comparatively few single women

insights.claim: For unmarried adults in their 30s, the top employed-single-men ratios shift to high-earning tech/professional hubs — Sunnyvale (CA), Ramsey and Franklin Lakes (NJ), Madison's suburbs (WI), and parts of Tucson (AZ) — anchored by concentrations of engineers, developers, and scientists that skew male.
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Tech-hub gender imbalance in engineering/STEM occupations creates a favorable marriage market specifically for women in their 30s — a demographic tailwind tied to the geography of the tech labor market.
insights.quote: these regions are anchored by concentrations of well-paid engineers, software developers, scientists, and other professional workers, occupations that tend to have more men than women in their thirties

insights.claim: A higher ratio of higher-earning (not just employed) single men to single women has a strong positive correlation with marriage rates for women in their 30s, but shows essentially no correlation with marriage rates for women ages 22-29.
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Income-based mate selection appears to sharpen with age — men's earnings matter much more for women choosing a spouse in their 30s than in their 20s, a nuance that complicates simple 'money attracts marriage' narratives.
insights.quote: the ratio of higher-earning men to single women has a strong, positive correlation with marriage rates among women in their thirties, but not women ages 22-29

insights.claim: North Central Detroit has the lowest ratio of full-time employed single men to single women among 20-somethings: only 31 employed men per 100 single women ages 22-29.
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Quantifies an extreme structural mismatch (roughly 1 employed single man per 3 single women) that helps explain persistently low marriage and family-formation rates in parts of Detroit.
insights.quote: North Central Detroit has the lowest ratio of full-time employed single men to all single women. For every 100 single women ages 22 to 29, there are only 31 employed men of the same age.

insights.claim: For adults in their 30s, the weakest marriage markets by employed-single-men ratio are Marion County, FL, and south-side Chicago neighborhoods (about 35 employed single men per 100 single women), along with parts of the Bronx, Brooklyn, and economically-distressed Dougherty/Lee Counties (GA) and Wayne County (MI).
insights.speaker: Wendy Wang, Ken Burchfiel and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Identifies specific economically-distressed geographies where the local marriage market is structurally the most difficult for women in their 30s, useful for targeting family-policy or workforce interventions.
insights.quote: there are only about 35 full‑time employed single men for every 100 single women
